title: This is my family
goal: Talk about your family, and use the possessives (*mein*, *dein*, *sein*, *ihr*) whose ending follows the gender of the thing owned — not the owner.
bekal: name the members of your family
say who something belongs to (*mein Bruder*, *meine Schwester*)
say you don't have something (*Ich habe keine Geschwister*)

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Familienfotos
dialogs.intro: Break time. Lena pulls out her phone, and Budi gets caught in the same ritual found in every language on earth: looking at someone else's family photos.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Schau mal, das ist meine Familie.
lines.literal: look once, that is my family.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Das sind meine Eltern. Mein Vater heißt Thomas, meine Mutter heißt Petra.
lines.id: Those are my parents. My father's name is Thomas, my mother's name is Petra.
lines.literal: that are my parents. my father is-called Thomas, my mother is-called Petra.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: And do you have any brothers or sisters?

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Ja, ich habe einen Bruder und zwei Schwestern.
lines.id: Yes, I have a brother and two sisters.
lines.literal: yes, I have a brother and two sisters.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Er ist zwanzig. Seine Frau heißt Mia. Sie haben ein Kind.
lines.id: He's twenty. His wife's name is Mia. They have a child.
lines.literal: he is twenty. his wife is-called Mia. they have a child.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Genau. Und du? Wie ist deine Familie?
lines.id: Exactly. And you? What's your family like?
lines.literal: exactly. and you? how is your family?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ich habe keine Geschwister. Ich bin Einzelkind.
lines.id: I don't have any brothers or sisters. I'm an only child.
lines.literal: I have no siblings. I am single-child.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Und deine Eltern? Wo wohnen sie?
lines.id: And your parents? Where do they live?
lines.literal: and your parents? where live they?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sie wohnen in Bandung. Ihr Haus ist klein, aber sehr gemütlich.
lines.id: They live in Bandung. Their house is small, but very cozy.
lines.literal: they live in Bandung. their house is small, but very cozy.

notes: ***mein* or *meine*? The thing owned decides, not the owner.** *Mein Vater* (masculine) but *meine Mutter* (feminine) — even though the owner is the same person. English *my* never changes, so this is the longest-lasting source of beginner mistakes.

***sein* for a male owner, *ihr* for a female owner.** Line 7: *Seine Frau* = **his** wife. If Lena were talking about her sister, she'd say *ihr Mann* = **her** husband. So far, just like English his/her — but then the ending (*-e* or nothing) marks the thing owned on top of that.

**Line 5: *einen Bruder*, not *ein Bruder*.** A masculine noun changes form as soon as it becomes the object of an action — here, the object of "have". This is called the **Akkusativ**, and it's taken apart fully in Unit 7. For now just note the pattern: *ich habe **einen** Bruder*, *ich habe **eine** Schwester*, *ich habe **ein** Kind*.
***Geschwister* is always plural.** It has no singular — if you have one sibling, you say *einen Bruder* or *eine Schwester*. The same goes for *die Eltern* (parents), which is never singular.
***Wie alt…?*** means "how old", and the answer uses *sein*, not *haben*: *Ich **bin** zwanzig* — just as in English, and not "I have twenty years" as in French or Spanish.
***Schau mal*** = "have a look". The word *mal* in the middle of a sentence softens a command into a relaxed invitation — *Komm mal!*, *Sag mal…* Without *mal*, the sentence sounds like an order.

grammars.title: haben (to have) — the second verb you must know by heart
body: Together with *sein*, this verb holds up half of German: it's used for possession, for hunger and thirst, and later — in Unit 17 — to build almost all of the past tense.
after: Only the two middle forms are irregular: *du hast* and *er hat* drop their **b**. The rest follow the regular verb pattern you set up in Unit 2.

Some everyday expressions use *haben* where English uses *be* + adjective: *Ich habe Hunger* ("I'm hungry", literally "I have hunger"), *Ich habe Durst* (I'm thirsty), *Ich habe Zeit* (I have time), *Ich habe keine Zeit* (I'm busy).

grammars.title: Possessives: one family, two endings
body: All possessives behave exactly like *ein* / *kein* — that's why grammar books call them *ein-Wörter*. There are only two endings: **nothing** for masculine & neuter, **-e** for feminine & plural.
after: ⚠️ The last three rows look almost identical, and that really is confusing at first: *ihr* can mean "her", "their", or — capitalized, *Ihr* — "your" (formal). Only context and the capital letter tell them apart. The good news: in conversation, the three rarely collide in the same sentence.
Notice also *euer* → *eure*: the **e** in the middle drops out as soon as an ending is added. The same thing happens with *unser* → *unsre* in fast speech, though *unsere* remains the written form.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Mein Freund* and *meine Freundin* have a double meaning: "my friend" or "my boyfriend / girlfriend". To make clear you mean just a friend, people say *ein Freund von mir* ("a friend of mine"). One word's difference, and a fairly costly misunderstanding.

blocks.text: The three sentences below use everything in this unit at once. Try changing the names to those of your own family and say them out loud — what sticks is material about your life, not Lena's.

items: *Meine Mutter heißt Siti. Sie ist fünfzig und sie arbeitet in Bandung.*
*Ich habe einen Bruder. Er heißt Rian und er ist Student.*
*Meine Eltern wohnen in Indonesien. Ihr Haus ist klein, aber sehr gemütlich.*

blocks.title: One habit that saves months
items: Every time you meet a new noun, say three things at once: its article, the word and its plural — *die Schwester, die Schwestern*.
If you write vocabulary in a notebook, write the article in a different color for each gender. The brain remembers colors far better than the letters d-e-r.
Never write a bare noun in your notes. *Bruder* alone is half the information, and the missing half is exactly what you'll need later.
Ich habe einen Bruder und zwei Schwestern.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the correct form of *haben*.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: This is my family. — Do you have any brothers or sisters? — I have a brother and two sisters. — How old is your father? — His wife's name is Mia. — I don't have time.
